title: Diffuse astrocytoma and the diagnostic dilemma of an unusual phenotype: A case report
case_prompt:
A 48-year-old man with a one-year history of hypertension on therapy presented with one day of right-sided weakness, facial palsy, and generalized tonic–clonic seizures lasting two minutes each. On examination, he was alert and oriented, with right upper and lower limb strength 4/5 and equivocal plantar responses.  
 
Noncontrast head CT showed a partially well-defined heterogeneous lesion in the posterior corpus callosum and septum pellucidum, a low-density ill-defined area in the left parietal lobe containing multiple high-density calcifications, and effacement of left cerebral sulci. Ischemic stroke was initially suspected, but the calcifications raised concern for tuberculous infection. The patient was treated with anticonvulsants, antibiotics, neurotrophic support, and was discharged after five days on ongoing antihypertensives and supportive medications.  
 
Two weeks later, he returned with loss of consciousness. Brain MRI on T1-weighted images demonstrated an irregular lesion involving the splenium of the corpus callosum extending into the left periventricular parietal lobe with cystic foci in the septum pellucidum, showing low signal intensity. T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences showed high signal intensity in the same regions. Post-gadolinium T1-weighted images revealed an irregularly outlined, heterogeneously enhancing “butterfly” lesion involving the body and splenium of the corpus callosum and extending into bilateral periventricular parietal lobes.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Ischemic stroke was considered because of acute focal deficits and CT findings — “Ischemic stroke was the primary suggested diagnosis, but the calcified foci suggested tuberculous infection as a differential diagnosis.”  
2. Tuberculous infection was considered due to intracranial calcifications — “the calcified foci suggested tuberculous infection as a differential diagnosis.”  
3. Primary CNS lymphoma was considered given corpus callosum involvement — “primary CNS lymphomas … typically appears as intermediate or low SI on T1WIs, high or intermediate SI on T2WIs with restricted diffusion on DWIs … and usually shows homogenous enhancement after contrast administration.”  
4. Glioblastoma multiforme was considered for its butterfly pattern and enhancement — “GBMs … show heterogeneous low SI on T1WIs, high SI on T2WIs with prominent internal necrosis … and it reveals irregular heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration.”  
5. Oligodendroglioma was included in the differential given calcifications on CT — “GBM multiform, oligodendroglioma and lymphoma were suggested as differential diagnoses.”  
6. Acute infarction of the corpus callosum was disfavored because of DWI/ADC characteristics — “the lesion was not restricted in DWIs and showed slightly high SI on the ADC map, further decreasing the likelihood of infarction.”  
7. Infection (tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, fungal) was excluded by metabolic markers and serology — “the presence of brain tissue markers … indicate a low likelihood of infection. Therefore, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis and fungal infection were not possible in the current case.”  
8. Toxoplasmosis was specifically ruled out with negative antibody testing — “the toxoplasmosis test was negative in both immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM).”
